A company named “ABC survey” is looking to build a small satellite of dimension 10x10x10 cm to be launched into sun synchronous polar orbit using PSLV launch vehicle in Jan 2028. Today is April 3, 2026 and you are a frontend developer on the web team at the City of Lakeridge Building and Development Services. Criteria test whether the code actually addresses the WCAG violations from the audit — not just whether any code was produced. A model that writes generic accessibility improvements without addressing the specific audit findings will fail most implicit criteria.

You are a lawyer at a law firm in Jacksonville, Florida.  A client of your firm, Jared, is a resident of Detroit, Michigan where he was an employee of HC Hospitals (“HC”).  Jared hired your firm in June 2025, to represent him in disputing a denial of his long-term disability benefits claim that he filed with Principal Financial Group (“Principal”).  Below are some relevant details:
-	HC provides long-term disability benefits to eligible employees under an employee welfare benefit plan (“the LTD Plan”) governed by ERISA. 
-	HC insures the LTD Plan benefits under an insurance policy with Principal. 
-	Principal is headquartered in Des Moines, Iowa.
-	Upon the advice of his doctors in Michigan, Jared filed a claim for benefits under the LTD Plan with Principal. 
-	Principal’s Minnesota claims office decided to approve Jared’s LTD claim, upon finding him totally disabled and entitled to benefits under the LTD Plan. 
-	A year later, Principal’s California claims office decided to terminate Jared’s LTD claim, upon finding him to no longer totally disabled and entitled to benefits under the LTD Plan. 
-	Jared filed an appeal, which Principal reviewed and denied out of its Iowa claims office, upon affirming the finding that Jared was no longer totally disabled and entitled to LTD Plan benefits. 
-	Principal’s regional claims office in Jacksonville, Florida was also involved in administering Jared’s claim. 
-	Jared still lives in Detroit, Michigan.  All of Jared’s treating doctors certifying his LTD claim are also in the Detroit, Michigan area.  
-	The LTD Plan provides for one level of administrative appeal review.

Your supervising partner at the firm is the lead attorney handling Jared’s case (“the Partner).  The Partner determined not to file any further administrative appeals, and proceeded to file an ERISA action in July 2025 disputing the denial of LTD Plan benefits on Jared’s behalf against Principal and HC in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida, where your firm is located. In August 2025, Principal filed a motion to transfer venue to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, where Jared is located.  

The Partner has asked that you draft a legal memo advising him on how the Court should rule on Defendants’ motion to transfer venue.  The memorandum should be four pages or less in a pdf document, and be formatted as follows: one-inch margins, double spaced, 12-point Times New Roman Font, and follow the IRAC format (Issue, Rule, Analysis, Conclusion) with bolded/underlined headings.  Blue book citation format must be used.  The memo should be addressed to the Partner, and drafted in a neutral, objective manner. 

When preparing the legal memo:
1.	Assume that: (i) there is no venue selection clause in the LTD Plan; (ii) and ensure that you identify whether any case law authority cited in the legal memo is persuasive or binding authority.
2.	Consider and refer to the materials attached, which should be incorporated into the memo.

You are an associate corporate counsel for Harmony Run, a rapidly growing new app development company located in Silicon Valley, California. 

You just received an email from your supervising attorney. It reads:

__________________________________

Hi,

I hope you had a great microdose session last night. Sorry I had to leave early due to my cold plunge this morning. 

I have a big project for you. 

We just got a memo from Jax. If you don't know who he is, he came up with some key ideas for PeakHuman last year. Now he's pushing his new idea--it's called RoomLedger. The basic idea is that it's a one-stop app for all financial/background verification needs. The first obvious target is landlords, but they also want to include roommate matching services. I think the app's edge is that it can provide highly granular search criteria and can verify the income/background so you know that the person is who they say they are, at least on objectively verifiable points. I guess if the landlord also uses the app the background/credit check will go much more smoothly and quickly as well. For more details, check out the business proposal memo, attached as RoomLedger.docx. Anyway, all I know is that I've talked with Jax here and there about this new project and I think the success of PeakHuman kind of got to his head. I don't think he's inclined to take any negative response, certainly not from us eggheads at Legal.

So here's your task. This is an ambitious app but we need to research what kind of legal issues it may trigger. You are our civil rights/consumer rights and consumer credit expert. I need you to provide me with a formal legal memorandum describing the top five potential legal issues you can spot. Provide a detailed explanation because we may need to fight Jax if we identify any real problems. Additionally, mark how serious each problem is (for example, critical, serious, minor) and suggest a legally viable workaround (such as product redesign, user disclosure/consent, compliance workflow, or abandoning the feature). The workaround should include a specific assessment of how likely it is to work and the risks that come with it. I'm attaching two cases I found while doing quick preliminary research--attached as Fair Housing Council I.pdf and Fair Housing Council II.pdf. Based on my reading of the cases, my understanding is that the fair housing rules for landlord-screening may be different from the rules of roommate-matching, so be sure to keep that distinction clear. 

You know the leadership, they don't want to hear mushy words like "maybe," "reasonable," "possibly," or "a good chance." We'll hear them whine that they're paying us for guessing. Explain the odds of prevailing and the risks using specific, real life terms or examples that will get through these guys' heads (and egos). 

Generate your response in a downloadable WORD document. Keep the response under 1,200 words. I’ll ask follow up questions if I need more detail. Nobody around here has time to read treatises. Whenever you make a legal assertion, conclusion or proposition, cite a controlling legal authority using Bluebook format, and add a direct quote of the relevant language from that authority in parentheses following the citation--this makes it easier for me to assess the strength of the authority's support. Of course, you know you should cite the strongest authority if possible (statute or SCOTUS decision, then circuit court decision, then district court decision for federal cases, state supreme court for state ones).

Feel free to come talk to me if you have any questions.

prompt:
Today is April 8, 2026 and you are a platform engineer on the infrastructure team at Northfield Analytics. Your team is migrating services from manual EC2 deployments to containerized workloads. The first service up is the Event Processing Service, a Python application that ingests clickstream events from client SDKs, enriches them with statistical scoring, and writes to Kafka and PostgreSQL.
Currently this thing runs on a single EC2 instance, deployed by SSHing in and doing a git pull. No CI/CD for production, no containers, no autoscaling. It works but it doesn't scale and every deploy is a manual risk.
You have three files from different teams. Platform_Migration_ADR.pdf is the architecture decision record from the platform lead describing the target state: EKS, GitHub Actions, Secrets Manager, the whole thing. Environment_Configuration_Matrix.xlsx is the DevOps team's spreadsheet with environment-specific config, secrets sources, resource allocations, and networking details for dev, staging, and production. Event_Service_Operations_Runbook.docx is from the engineer who actually runs this service day to day, documenting how it's deployed now, what breaks, performance numbers, and known issues.
These three files were written by different people at different times and they do not agree with each other. Ports, health check paths, resource needs, how secrets are managed, even what CI/CD tool is in use for staging. Your job is to produce an implementation package that actually works given the real-world constraints, not just what the ADR idealistically describes.
Produce the following deliverables:
A production-ready Dockerfile with multi-stage build optimized for the service's Python dependencies. A docker-compose.yml for local development and for staging (since staging doesn't use Kubernetes yet). Kubernetes manifests for production: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret references, HPA, and PDB. A CI/CD pipeline definition for GitHub Actions covering lint, test, build, scan, push, deploy, and smoke test. A .env.example showing all required environment variables. Deployment documentation that explains every conflict you found between the three source files, what decision you made, and why. The documentation should also cover the operational concerns from the runbook that affect containerization, specifically the memory behavior, the shutdown problem, the startup time, and the connection pooling issue.
Do not ignore problems. If the ADR says the container should start in 30 seconds but the runbook says it takes 60, that's a conflict you need to address in your implementation. If the ADR's memory limits will cause OOM kills based on what the runbook reports, fix the limits and explain why you're deviating from the ADR. If staging uses Docker Compose on a single box while production uses Kubernetes, you need both.

prompt:
It's May 2, 2026, and you're a private equity associate on the consumer team. Your MD asked you to build an LBO model for a take-private of a public footwear company and put together a one-pager with your recommendation on if the firm should go forward with the buyout. The firm already owns 10% of the company's public shares and this will roll over into the new equity at the offer price. Only use the file attached, LBO_Inputs.xlsx. Don't use any outside information. If an input required for a calculation is missing, leave the output that's affected blank and flag it in an Issues Log.

Create 2 files, an Excel file called LBO_Model.xlsx and a Word document called Investment_Memo.docx. In the Excel, use formulas for the calculations, only the inputs can be hardcoded.

The LBO model’s analysis should tell my MD the following info:

1. Sources & uses: Build a sources and uses table for the LBO. The current share price and offer premium are in LBO_Inputs.xlsx. Account for the firm's existing 10% stake rolling over at the offer price as a no-cash equity contribution.

2. Operating model: Project a 5-year operating model from FY2026 to FY2030 covering revenue, EBITDA, net income, FCFs, etc. Use the drivers from LBO_Inputs.xlsx.

3. Debt: Keep this section simple with just a Term Loan B and a Revolver. For each year, show the balances, amortization, sweep, interest (use average balance).

4. Returns: Calculate MOIC and IRR on total equity (rolled plus new equity). The exit will be at the end of FY2030 at the exit EV/EBITDA multiple in LBO_Inputs.xlsx. Show the bridge from exit enterprise value to sponsor proceeds and also show this on a waterfall chart.

5. Sensitivity tables: Build 2, 5x5 2-variable sensitivity tables. Both will show exit EV/EBITDA multiple and revenue growth changes. 1 table will calculate MOIC, and the other calculates IRR.

6. Chart: Create 1 chart showing revenue, FCFs, and total debt outstanding for FY2026 through FY2030.

7. Tie-outs: Include pass/fail checks that check if (i) sources equal uses, (ii) UFCF adds up correctly, and (iii) exit equity proceeds add up correctly.

8. Issues log: Any calculations that are affected due to missing data or info, write them here.

Make the investment memo 1 page long and include:

1. A buy or pass recommendation in the header (If the model gets 20%+ IRR).

2. A deal summary.

3. The investment thesis.

4. A key metrics table (entry EV, multiples, leverage, returns, etc.)

5. Key risks

prompt:
It's April 27, 2026, and you're an investment banking analyst on the consumer team. Your VP asked you to build a DCF for a consumer goods company. Only use the files attached, Company_Inputs.xlsx and DCF_Assumptions.xlsx. Don’t use any outside information. If an input required for a calculation is missing, leave the output that's affected blank and flag it in an Issues Log.

Create 1 Excel file called Company_DCF.xlsx. Use formulas for the calculations, only the inputs can be hardcoded.

The analysis in the Excel file should tell my VP the following info:

1. Valuation with different scenarios: Build a 5-year DCF (FY2026 to FY2030) under 3 cases, base, bear, and bull. Bear and bull cases have to come from the base case using the adjustment rows found in DCF_Assumptions.xlsx.

2. Operating model: Project out revenue, EBITDA, D&A, EBIT, tax, NOPAT, Capex, change in NWC, and UFCF. Use the drivers (like margin and percent of revenue drivers) found in DCF_Assumptions.xlsx.

3. WACC and terminal value: Calculate the WACC from the provided inputs (don’t hardcode it). The terminal value will use the exit multiple method using the EV/EBITDA multiple. Include bear and bull case adjustments.

4. Equity value bridge: Show the bridge from enterprise value to equity value using the net debt and shares data from Company_Inputs.xlsx and show the implied share price for each of the 3 scenarios. Also create a waterfall chart showing the bridge from enterprise value to equity value for the base case.

5. Sensitivity tables: Have a 5x5, 2-variable sensitivity table that shows the implied share price under various exit EV/EBITDA multiples and WACCs. Multiple steps will be the base multiple multiple +/- 0.5x, and WACC will be the WACC +/- 0.5%.

6. Cross scenario checker: Add a table that checks every year that the bear case growth is equal to the base case growth plus the bear case adjustment. Do the same for bull case. Show the numeric difference and include a pass/fail indicator to make sure it’s all correct.

7. Tie-outs: Include a pass/fail check that tests if UFCF adds up with all of its components and that the present value of UFCF plus the present value of the terminal value is equal to the enterprise value for each of the 3 scenarios.

8. Issues log: Any calculations that are affected due to missing data or info, log it here.

prompt:
You are an information systems manager at a regional children’s retail company that is rebuilding its customer-facing web portal. The company sells toys, games, books, learning kits, birthday gifts, baby products, and seasonal items through stores and online ordering. Leadership wants the portal to feel simple for parents and gift buyers, but also safer, more reliable, and easier for store and support teams to manage during holidays, back-to-school season, and birthday promotions.

The current website was built in pieces over time, with items like product search, store pickup, gift registries, loyalty rewards, customer support, and order tracking not sharing a consistent account, inventory, or support workflow. Customers repeat information across pages, store associates deal with pickup orders before inventory is truly confirmed, and support teams receive avoidable questions about order status, returns, age-appropriate products, and product safety.

The input file kids_store_portal_notes.pdf contains stakeholder notes, current website pain points, customer complaints, system notes, desired portal features, inventory concerns, safety and privacy issues, early journey notes, leadership goals, unresolved tradeoffs, and open architecture questions. Use this file as the basis for a customer-facing web portal architecture and design document, where the document should explain the current-state issues, proposed future-state portal architecture, major user journeys, systems involved, integration points, data flows, privacy and security expectations, operational risks, and management decisions needed before implementation begins. The portal design should account for common customer tasks such as browsing by age and interest, searching for toys, checking store availability, placing online orders, choosing pickup or delivery, managing registries, using loyalty rewards, reviewing product safety information, tracking orders, handling returns, and contacting support. It should also explain how internal systems such as ecommerce, inventory, point of sale, CRM, loyalty, payment processing, fulfillment, product information, and customer support should coordinate behind the scenes.

A main challenge is that parents need the portal to be fast and easy, while the business needs accurate inventory, safe handling of child-related data, clear product safety ownership, and reliable operational controls. If a convenience feature creates privacy, safety, inventory, or support-risk concerns, call out the tradeoff and recommend a controlled approach. Address the open architecture questions raised in kids_store_portal_notes.pdf with a recommended approach and rationale. This should include decisions about pickup availability ownership, low-inventory behavior, account unification across loyalty/registry/checkout, required product content before publishing, recall and safety update flow, support-agent data access, and degraded behavior when loyalty or payment systems are slow during peak traffic.

This is a systems-management and architecture deliverable, not a frontend implementation task. The final document should be understandable to business leaders, store operations, customer support, merchandising, legal/privacy reviewers, and technical teams. Deliver a customer-facing web portal architecture and design document in .docx format. This document should cover current-state issues from kids_store_portal_notes.pdf, the target portal architecture, customer journeys, system integrations, data flow, product-information governance, privacy and safety controls, accessibility considerations, operational risks, phased rollout plan, success measures, and the recommended decisions for unresolved architecture questions.

prompt:
A local Public Housing Authority in Illinois is proposing to install smart meters, which are electric meters usually installed and operated by utility companies. While initially their primary purpose was to allow utility companies to collect meter data without having to have a reader physically come every billing period, smart meters have become sophisticated equipment that can read and wirelessly transmit highly granular power usage information. Essentially, this enables the account holder and the utility company to monitor the power every few minutes and study patterns, leakages or potential abuses.

This PHA subsidizes some, but not all, of the tenants' utility payments, including electricity (depends on income). The PHA management is highly interested in smart meters because some of the recipients are bad apples and engage in activities that are wasteful or even criminal. Some tenants are known to grow marijuana using heat lamps or harvest cryptocurrencies. The management is especially offended by those tenants because they use taxpayer subsidized electricity to generate illegal income, and still reside in tax subsidized housing when their actual income (thanks to their illegal activities) may be far above the eligibility limit, when the waiting list is full of families in real need. 

The PHA management is aware from previous legal consultation that they can't just ask the utility company to provide them with the smart meter data. The recommendation was that they amend  the lease agreement to specifically include a provision that gives the PHA right to access the smart meter data and if necessary hand it to the police. The new lease would be signed when existing tenants renew their certification (biannually), as well as when new applicants are accepted. 

Present a draft of the provision that is most likely to be held valid by the court. The provision should not be more than four sentences long, because I don't want it to attract too much attention. For the same reason, avoid using the words "police," "law enforcement" or "crime" in that provision. 

Then provide a Fourth Amendment analysis explaining why you've chosen to draft the provision the way you did, and specifically address what you did to make sure it will not be held invalid under Carpenter v. U.S., 585 U.S. 296 (2018) or Naperville Smart Meter Awareness v. City of Naperville*, 900 F.3d 521 (7th Cir. 2018). Finally, provide an analysis of the likelihood that the provision will be held invalid, and the most practical way to mitigate that risk.

Generate your response in WORD document using 12-point New Times Roman font, as that's my typical practice. Follow the standard legal memo format and limit your response to 600 words. After every sentence making a legal assertion, assessment or conclusion, cite a supporting legal authority using the bluebook format. If possible, cite the strongest authority (SCOTUS then Seventh Circuit). If citing non-controlling authority, specify that in your response. Make the document as practical as possible and avoid using vague terms like "reasonable," "generally," "diligent," "good effort," or "adequate" for your recommendations. 

Finally, there's no need to go over the general consent to search doctrine as we've already discussed that, unless you can make a point that directly applies to this situation.
